prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks remain my first choice after reading the full set of opening ballots. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the trade-off between trapping many atoms and perturbing the clock transition, and Ye's group then showed that this idea delivers record stability and accuracy, including control of many-body interactions in a degenerate Fermi gas. The result is a measurement capability that did not exist before, with consequences for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the planned redefinition of the second. It is also the only top-ranked candidate on which six of seven ranking members place it in their top three, with unanimous agreement on the two credited names. The attribution is clean, the work has been reproduced and surpassed in many laboratories over two decades, and the interpretation is stable. None of that is true of the other leading candidates to the same degree. I do not treat the breadth of opening support as proof of merit, but here the scientific arguments in the ballots (originality, clarity, independent confirmation) are consistent with it.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and precision spectroscopy and the 2012 prize for control of single trapped ions, which together cover the neighbouring ground. A reasonable colleague could say that lattice clocks are the next refinement of a recognised line rather than a new discovery about nature. The second objection is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the practical payoff is still prospective, and that other groups (PTB, NIST, SYRTE, Sr and Yb clock groups, and the ion-clock community) made real contributions that the two credited names do not cover. I think the first objection is answered by the fact that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept and the accuracy gain of several orders of magnitude over the prior generation is a qualitative change, but I accept that it is a judgement and not a proof.

responses.point: Ranks IceCube first as a clue found in nature that opened a new observational window, and ranks the lattice clocks second as original, mature and clearly attributed.
responses.response: I agree that B004 is a clean two-name case and I take his emphasis on discovery in nature seriously. My reservation about B032 is attribution and maturity of the interpretation, not the instrument. The diffuse flux is established, but the origin of the flux is not understood, and the source associations are at modest significance. Allocating three names among Halzen, Karle, Yoshida and a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA predecessors, is a real unresolved problem; I would credit only Halzen and Karle if forced, and that already shows the allocation is not settled. I also note that his own ballot says he relied on background knowledge for the roles. Lattice clocks do not carry that weakness, so I would still place them ahead, while keeping IceCube as a strong later candidate once the sources are better understood.

responses.point: Ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing that the prediction plus the 2018 experiment created moire materials, and proposes only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero.
responses.response: I share her view that B010 is a major discovery and I ranked it third. Her two-person proposal is also a useful qualification of the three-name credit, because it avoids the question of Bistritzer's share by leaving him out, but that creates its own difficulty: the continuum-model prediction is a joint paper, and dropping a co-author needs a justification that the evidence does not give. My larger concern is maturity. The pairing mechanism is still debated and the field is less than a decade old, so the discovery is secure but the lasting scientific outcome is not. Recognising it now carries a real risk that the citation will age badly. I do not think her argument that recognition is timely is wrong, but I weigh the unsettled mechanism more heavily, and clocks are settled in a way twisted bilayer graphene is not.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first as the architecture behind superconducting processors, and ranks lattice clocks last in his top eight mainly because of overlap with earlier precision-spectroscopy and ion-control prizes.
responses.response: His overlap concern about clocks is the one I take most seriously, since it is my own main reservation, and I do not dismiss it. Where I differ is that the same argument applies more strongly to B034: the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits, so honouring circuit architecture one year later is a closer repeat than clocks after 2005 and 2012. B034 also has four credited names for three places, so Blais or Girvin has to be excluded, and I proposed Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf in my opening, whereas most colleagues exclude Blais. That split is itself a sign the allocation is not fair as it stands. He is right that circuit QED is excellent physics, but I would not give priority to it now.

responses.point: Ranks dynamical mean-field theory first as the first controlled non-perturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, with Georges, Vollhardt and Kotliar as a natural trio.
responses.response: I respect the argument that DMFT is a durable framework, but I find the attribution in his own text weaker than he states it. He credits Metzner and Vollhardt for the infinite-dimension limit and Georges, Kotliar, Krauth and Rozenberg for the impurity mapping; the proposed trio drops Metzner while keeping Vollhardt, and omits Muller-Hartmann, Krauth and Rozenberg. He also notes that Nobel precedent for methods is mixed. Being the only member to rank B027 means that none of the other seven has argued for it, so I cannot assess it as a shortlist leader. If it is to be considered I would want a colleague to show it explains a specific observation, as opposed to being a calculational tool, which is the same standard I apply to the attosecond and many-body methods I work on.

responses.point: Ranks lattice clocks first for reasons of measurement precision and ranks Hubbard-model quantum simulation with cold atoms second, proposing Bloch, Greiner and Zoller.
responses.response: We agree on B004 and on the names Katori and Ye, and we also agree on the Bloch, Greiner and Zoller trio for B016, which only the two of us ranked. I regard it as a credible alternative, but I would be honest about its weaknesses. B016 overlaps with B023 on Cirac and Zoller, so the two cannot both be funded without sharing names, and Cirac's omission is a real attribution gap, as he notes. The result is mainly an enabling technique with the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram still open. That is why I keep it as an alternative and not as my preferred prize.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues judge lattice clocks sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes to count as a new discovery.
How much credit for the lattice-clock concept and performance belongs to other proposers and clock groups outside the two credited names; I cannot verify this from the supplied text.
Whether the redefinition of the second, which has not yet occurred, should be treated as a condition or only as a supporting argument.
Whether a two-part prize combining clocks with a second distinct achievement would be fairer than a single part; I have not found a pairing that clearly improves the allocation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile regarding Katori and Ye, whom my profile does not list as collaborators. My documented connections (Anne L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group, Dahlström, Argenti, Schuch, Indelicato) do not match any credited name on the shortlist, but I am an atomic physicist working close to B004, B016 and B023, and colleagues may want to note that proximity of field.
